lines.note: Completes foſſocu, ſu across the page boundary: hossoku, to set out, glossed izzuru, to emerge or depart. Sair como pera aguerra specifies going out for war; the repeated ſu at the foot of f213 is a catchword, not a second occurrence in the sentence.
The Portuguese &c. closes the preceding example of setting out. It is a genuine short continuation row, unlike the repeated catchword on the preceding page.

runs.text: Certa ſeita que veo da China.

lines.note: Hossōjū, a sect said to have come from China; NINJAL also identifies Fossǒjù. Enlargement separates a long ſ and a short s, not the OCR's fr. Preserve final jù and the printed caron rather than imposing modern shū or a uniform ss allograph.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de vara com que tan-

lines.note: Hossu: first a kind of rod for driving animals. Hũa maneira de vara introduces the implement, with tangem divided across rows; the two upright long s characters are retained.

runs.text: gem os bois, ou caualos que puxão pello carro.

lines.note: Tangem os bois, ou caualos describes driving the oxen or horses pulling the cart. This first practical sense should not be replaced with the Buddhist whisk sense supplied next.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Certa vara de que vſão os Ienxus

lines.note: The second sense is a staff used by Ienxus, Zen adherents. The Japanese-derived plural remains visibly italic within Portuguese, rather than being automatically changed to roman.
Em ſuas ceremonias completes the ritual use of the implement. The possessive refers to the Zen practitioners in the previous row.

runs.text: Pao grande, ou aruore caida no chão,

lines.note: Hota, a large piece of wood or a fallen tree. Pao and aruore are the printed historical spellings; caida no chão specifies lying on the ground.
The qualification & podre adds that the wood is rotten. This short physical row continues hota rather than forming a separate entry.
Hotade is the flower of tade, the plant named in the Portuguese definition. Tade is italic here despite being Japanese vocabulary.
Hōtai is equated with hachi, a bee, and Portuguese Abelha confirms the insect. The circumflex and the separate explanatory i, are preserved.
Hotaru, a firefly, corresponds directly to Portuguese Cagalume. Neither the Japanese f nor the old Portuguese compound needs modernization.

runs.text: Certo genero de lapas, cuja caſca

lines.note: Hotategai, scallop, is described broadly as a kind of shellfish. The next rows explain using its shell as a ladle; the Japanese g is appropriate for gai, 貝.

runs.text: ſerue de vieira pera tirar Xiru, ou caldo da

lines.note: The shell serves to take xiru, shiru or broth, from a pot. Xiru is visibly italic within Portuguese; vieira is retained rather than silently substituting a modern utensil name.
Panella completes the reference to the cooking pot. Its doubled l is part of the printed Portuguese spelling.

runs.text: Eſpaço, ou lugar no meo da barriga

lines.note: Hotebara denotes the middle area of the belly. Espaço, ou lugar no meo da barriga defines a bodily location, with meo retained as printed.
Do homem closes the anatomical definition. The crop contains the complete short row and the tops of neighboring text only as context.
Hōteki, 放擲, is glossed nageuchi, u, to throw away. Arremeſar, ou lar continues as largar on the next row; no hyphen is supplied where the crop does not show one.

runs.text: gar da mão algua couſa que ſe eſta fazendo.

lines.note: Largar da mão means dropping or abandoning something one is doing. Algua lacks a secure nasal mark here; retain the scan reading instead of normalizing it to algũa.
Banji wo hōteki suru means abandoning everything. The caron in fǒteqi distinguishes this entry from the following Fôteqi in the source notation.
Largar mão de tudo finishes the Portuguese explanation of giving everything up. Preserve the physical split lar-/gar rather than merging rows.
Hōteki, 法敵, opponents of the law or doctrine. The circumflex contrasts with the preceding throwing-away word; the compact Portuguese definition supports a distinct entry.

Hotguanxin is a contracted Buddhist compound for arousing a vow or aspiration; negai wo okosu kokoro supplies the transparent Japanese explanation. The final t in Fot- is not to be expanded in Level 1.
Coração pio, & deuoto describes a pious, devoted heart. Co-/ração is a physical line split, not an independent Japanese syllable.
Hotjo, glossed harai nozoku, means clearing or shaking something away. Lançar fora, ou ſacudir supports the reading and the retained contracted t before j.

The literal example is shaking out dust; Permet. then signals the metaphorical application below. The second scan pass shows two o letters in poo, an older spelling of modern pó, retained without an editorial accent.

Varu nozomi wo hotjo suru is explained as casting away bad desires. Enlargement shows Varu followed by a space, not Varuunozomi; do not add an unprinted adjectival i merely because modern warui is expected.
Sacudir fora ruins deſejos confirms the moral rather than physical application. The continuation ſa-/cudir is preserved at its physical break.

runs.text: O vir, ou ter algũa febre. ¶

lines.note: Hotnet, 発熱, the onset or presence of fever. The Portuguese word is febre, not ſebre: both the sense and the crossbar support f. Fot- begins the repeated verbal example.
Fotnet ſuru turns the preceding noun into the verb 'to develop a fever'; Idem refers back to that definition. The contracted final t remains source text.
Hōtō, 法灯, the lamp or light of doctrine, glossed nori no tomoxibi. Both accents are circumflexes on enlargement, consistent with NINJAL Fôtô; this is not Fôtǒ.
Hōtō wo kakaguru means raising the doctrinal lamp. The repeated word likewise has two circumflexes; the following Eſpa- begins espalhar, spreading that light.

runs.text: lhar, ou communicar a luz da lei prègando a,

lines.note: Communicating the light by preaching explains the figurative lamp. Keep prègando and the separated a as printed rather than modernizing Portuguese orthography.

runs.text: &c. ¶ Item, Acender lume como a lam-

lines.note: A second application is literally lighting a lamp. Acender lume como a lam- connects directly to lampada in the next physical row.
The lamp stands before a Fotoque, a Buddhist image. Fotoque is italic in this Portuguese sentence and should remain so, with a review toggle available.

Hotobakaxi, ſu, aita is the transitive softening verb. A stain covers much of the a in aita, but the remaining shape, conjugational context, and NINJAL support aita rather than iita; the damage is not a separate letter.

runs.text: lecer algũa couſa metendoa na agoa, &c.

lines.note: Putting something in water to soften it completes the transitive definition. Agoa and metendoa are preserved historical forms, not corrected to modern água/metendo-a.
Hotobi, uru, ita is the corresponding intransitive 'become soft'. The Portuguese is abrandarſe, not abrandas ſe; the infinitive and scan agree on r before the reflexive suffix.
The object becomes soft in water. Agua is printed differently from agoa two rows earlier; both forms are retained without harmonization.
Hotocuri is simply identified as a named herb. The Portuguese formula reads aßi chamada, not aßrchamada; the i and word boundary are visible.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de ſoar a janela,

lines.note: Hotofototo is an adverb describing the sound of a window or door. Read ſoar, 'to sound', rather than ſoer; Adu. remains italic as printed.

runs.text: ou porta, &c. quando ſe bate a ella. Vt

lines.note: The sound occurs when the door or window is struck. Vt introduces a Japanese example, and its italic style is preserved.
Hotofototo to wo utsu means knocking on a door with that sound. Portuguese Bater na porta confirms the construction; dã- continues as dando below.
Dando pancadas finishes the description of striking or knocking. The short continuation is complete in its crop.
Hotogui, a jar or pot, begins a proverbial example. The repeated word is Fotoguiuo, hotogi wo, not Fotoguin o; enlargement shows the u shape and Japanese object particle.

Comutte kabeni mukō ga gotoxi describes having the jar over one's head while facing a wall. The first vowel looks o, so comutte is retained rather than modernized to kabutte; the Portuguese continuation establishes the intended scene.

runs.text: maneira de hum que eſta virado pera apare-

lines.note: A maneira de hum introduces the comparison with someone turned toward a wall. The sentence continues into column 2; no separate entry begins at that boundary.

runs.text: de com hũa jarra metida na cabeça.

lines.note: Completes parede and specifies a jar placed over the person's head. This clarifies the preceding Japanese proverb and confirms the cross-column continuation.
Hotondo is equated with oyoso, 'for the most part'. The initial V in Voyoſo represents the Japanese vowel sequence rather than a Portuguese consonant.
Mais frequentemente gives the additional sense 'more frequently'. This belongs to hotondo, not the plant entry below.
Hotoke no za names a plant and, in a second sense, a Buddha's seat. The printed Aſ- continues as aſſento; it is not a second headword.

runs.text: ſento, ou trono do Fotoque que he à maneira

lines.note: The throne or seat of the Fotoque is shaped like a flower. Read he, the historical copula, rather than be; Fotoque remains italic in the Portuguese explanation.
Flor do golfão specifies a water-lily-like flower. The gloss is a source description, not a reason to impose a modern botanical classification.

runs.text: Borda de algũa couſa, ou junto, &c.

lines.note: Hotori means an edge or vicinity. Borda de algũa couſa, ou junto gives both senses; no change to the printed nasal spelling is needed.
Michi no hotori is the edge or vicinity of a road. The Japanese example and Portuguese Borda, ou junto do are aligned in the crop.
Caminho completes the road example. This short physical row is retained independently.
Hototoguisu, the cuckoo, is introduced as a named bird. Preserve the source's long ſ in the Japanese word and the joined ß in aßi rather than conflating their typographic forms.
Its voice is sad and plaintive: ſaudoſa, not the OCR's ſandeſa. Enlarging the faded middle supports au/do, and the Portuguese adjective fits the bird's song.
Hotowori, u, otta describes having a fever. The abbreviated u is printed even though the paradigm may suggest a fuller ending; retain it rather than regularize.
The usage is particularly for children's fever. Mininos is the source spelling and not an OCR error for meninos to be normalized.
Hotoworike is a childhood fever illness. Doença is visibly present, with the e omitted by OCR; the correction is supported by the standard noun and scan.
Hotoworike ni gozaru means being ill with fever. The honorific/existential construction is ordinary Japanese and agrees with Eſtar doente.
De febres completes the illness definition. The row has no Japanese text requiring a kana hint.

Fotro teiqiǔ is a literary expression for weeping and shedding tears. The unusual Fotro sequence is retained: NINJAL records the same form, so it is not silently rewritten as a more familiar compound.

runs.text: O raparſe, ou fazerſe rapado como

lines.note: Hottai concerns shaving the head or becoming a tonsured person. The definition develops into religious withdrawal rather than merely cutting hair.

runs.text: ſe coſtuma em Iapão. ¶ Item, Peßoa que ſe

lines.note: The practice is said to be customary in Iapão. The initial capital is I, not lowercase l; the second meaning begins 'a person who…'.
The person shaves or leaves worldly life; Fottai ſuru supplies the verbal form. The long ſ in ſuru is retained from the scan.
Raparſe, ou fazerſe rapado completes the verbal definition. These reflexive Portuguese forms refer to taking the tonsure.
Hottan here denotes the depths of the heart, not automatically the modern sense 'beginning'. The following example begins hottan yori, 'from the heart'.
Hottan yori toga okuri wo suru describes willingly making amends for faults. Preserve the printed vocuri rather than replacing it with an inferred modern lexical form.
The Portuguese confirms heartfelt satisfaction or reparation for sins. ſatisfação retains f rather than a second long ſ; no theological expansion is inserted into the transcription.
Hottoku means understanding or realization; hottoku xite is its conjunctive form. The Portuguese En continues into entendendo without adding an unseen hyphen.
Tendendo finishes entendendo, 'understanding'. The physical split is retained even though the first row has no hyphen.
Howata is the belly or bulging part of a sail. Bojo da vela supplies the nautical sense directly.

runs.text: Rei velho que renunciou ja o reino no

lines.note: Hōō is described as an old ruler who has already ceded the kingdom. Both carons are clear and should not be harmonized with the following phoenix entry.
The kingdom has been ceded to the ruler's son. Filho completes the previous sentence, not a new definition.
Hōō, the phoenix, is glossed 'bird of the sun'. The first accent is circumflex and the second caron, a source distinction from the preceding royal title.
Hōon, 報恩, repaying kindness, glossed on wo hōzuru. The accent over fôzuru is visible and was omitted by OCR; the repayment sense agrees with retribuir beneficios.
Hōon ni tsukayuru means serving in gratitude. The nasal abbreviation ẽ begins the Portuguese phrase 'in satisfaction of…'.
Service repays benefits received. Read ſatisfação, not ſatisſação: the second consonant has the f crossbar and is required by the Portuguese word.
A different hōon denotes generous benefits, glossed kōbaxii megumi. Preserve carons in Fǒuon and Cǒbaxij rather than importing the preceding entry's circumflex.
Hōon wo kōmuru means receiving favor. The Portuguese mercès and Japanese carons are visible and retained.
& fauores completes the expression for receiving favors. The printed v is retained without modernizing the spelling.

runs.text: Botar fora, ou lançar de ſi.

lines.note: Howori, ru, otta means casting something away. The paradigm and Portuguese Botar fora, ou lançar de ſi agree without a lexical correction.
Hoxa is a magician or sorcerer, marked by X. The label and its full stop are roman together; remove the OCR's spurious italic boundary around only the stop.
Hoxa here is the medical pair of replenishing and purging, glossed voguinai xaſuru. Refazer, & re- introduces the corresponding Portuguese therapeutic explanation.
Reſoluer com mezinhas completes the medical sense. Mezinhas means remedies; it should not be read as a modern unrelated noun or changed because of the old spelling.
Hōxa, a decorated ceremonial vehicle, is glossed takara no kuruma. The source accent is circumflex, confirmed by enlargement and NINJAL Fôxa, not the OCR caron.
The decorated carriage serves as andas, a carrying platform or litter. Ser/ue is split without an inserted hyphen.
Hōsei means praise or an esteemed name. The accent is worn but its surviving shape, the repeated fǒxei below, and NINJAL support caron; nome corrects the OCR's neme.
Biyo hōsei denotes a good name and reputation. The clear caron in fǒxei supports the preceding worn headword; S. remains an italic label.
A separate hōsei denotes generous kindness or benefaction, glossed kōbaxii nasake. The gloss distinguishes it from the preceding reputation word without changing source spelling.

runs.text: as obras honrando a peßoa de quem ſe recebẽ.

lines.note: Good deeds are received with honor toward the giver. Preserve peßoa and recebẽ, including the nasal abbreviation, rather than expanding the text.
Go-hōsei ni azzucaru means receiving gracious favors. Read azzucaru, not zzzucaru: the faded initial a and the Japanese verb agree; bo- continues on f215.
Catchword as repeats the first syllable on f215 and belongs to page furniture. It does not add a second as to the continuous Portuguese sentence.
